title: You Keep Asking God to Remove the Craving While Refusing to Tell One Safe Person It Exists
paragraphs:
You Keep Asking God to Remove the Craving While Refusing to Tell One Safe Person It Exists
Maybe the prayer you keep whispering in private is being followed by a step you keep refusing to take in the light.
That is what makes this so painful.

You were not playing games with God when you said it. You were tired. Ashamed. Frustrated with yourself. Maybe disgusted by how something you promised would never control you somehow learned your schedule, your weaknesses, your lonely hours, your triggers, your excuses.
You stayed clean for a while.
A night when nobody was watching.
Back in the place you swore you would never return to.
Because now you had to wake up the next morning and become the version of yourself everybody else knows.
Maybe you lifted your hands during worship while carrying a secret you were terrified somebody might discover.
People asked how you were doing.
And somewhere beneath that answer was another sentence:
“If they really knew me, would they still love me?”
So you kept praying for God to remove something you were determined to make sure no trustworthy human being ever knew existed.
And perhaps this is where Scripture needs to interrupt us.
To bring us into the light.
“Therefore confess your sins to one another…”
There is something profoundly Christian here that our private, image-conscious culture often resists.
James does not describe a faith where believers merely maintain appearances around one another.
He describes believers who tell the truth and pray for one another.
This does not mean you are commanded to announce your most intimate struggles publicly.
It does not mean posting your secret on Facebook.
It does not mean handing vulnerable information to unsafe, abusive, manipulative, immature, or gossiping people.
And it certainly does not mean that telling somebody about an addiction will automatically make every craving disappear.
Scripture gives us no license to promise that.
Christianity was never designed to be lived entirely behind a locked door.
Some of us want freedom without exposure.
We want somebody to pray for us without ever telling them what they are actually praying about.
Stuff cannot change somebody's opinion of you.
Stuff cannot force you to say:
“I keep taking something to numb myself.”
“I keep looking at things I hate myself for looking at.”
“I keep doing something I have begged God to help me stop doing.”
“I think this has become bigger than I can handle alone.”
Because secrecy makes a strange promise:
But secrecy often charges enormous interest for that protection.
It divides your public life from your private life.
It teaches you to manage appearances instead of receiving help.
It gives temptation a room where nobody else is allowed to turn on the light.
And eventually, you may become more afraid of being discovered than you are desperate to become free.
That is a frightening place to live.
You can know Bible verses there.
You can sing worship songs there.
You can have thousands of Christian followers there.
You can sit beside your spouse there.
And still be terrified that somebody might pick up your phone.
The scandal is not simply that Christians can struggle.
The scandal is how skilled we can become at looking spiritually healthy while quietly bleeding behind the costume.
But Jesus has never been frightened by the truth about you.
Before Peter denied Him, Jesus knew.
Before the Samaritan woman finished explaining her relationship history, Jesus knew.
Before Zacchaeus climbed down from the tree, Jesus knew.
Before Saul became Paul, Jesus knew exactly what Saul had done.
Before you whispered your latest confession, Christ already knew the thing you were trying to explain.
The Gospel is not good news because Jesus saves people who successfully hid their scandal.
The Gospel is good news because Jesus saves sinners.
At the cross, Christ did not die for your edited biography.
Sinners who need mercy they cannot manufacture.
“For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.”
Not after we finally became worthy of being associated with Him.
But grace is not permission to make peace with chains.
Jesus forgives us, and the grace that forgives also calls us out of darkness.
Notice again how difficult it is to separate walking in the light from fellowship.
The Gospel reconciles us to God through Christ, and it draws us into a people where truth no longer has to be our enemy.
Maybe that is why your secrecy deserves examination.
Not because every private struggle must become public knowledge.
But because there is a difference between privacy and secrecy used to protect destructive behavior.
Healthy privacy says, “Not everybody has earned access to this.”
Destructive secrecy says, “Nobody can ever know, because if somebody knows, they may interrupt what is controlling me.”
So perhaps the next prayer is not only:
“Jesus, give me courage to stop protecting the darkness.”
And then comes the frightening part.
A mature believer who demonstrates wisdom, discretion, compassion, biblical faithfulness, and enough courage to tell you the truth.
A trusted brother or sister in Christ.

And where addiction, withdrawal, trauma, self-harm, abuse, medical danger, or severe psychological distress is involved, trustworthy professional help may be an essential part of seeking care. Asking for help is not evidence that prayer failed.
You can pray while receiving counseling.
You can trust Christ while attending recovery meetings.
You can read Scripture while installing accountability systems.
You can repent while changing access, routines, environments, and relationships that continually feed the pattern.
Faithfulness is not measured by how little help you require.
Just the truth necessary to stop pretending.
And suddenly the secret that has been screaming inside your head has been spoken in the presence of another human being who loves Christ.
Maybe nothing miraculous happens in that instant.
Maybe the craving does not evaporate.
Maybe there are relapses that require deeper intervention.
The Bible does not teach us to confuse confession with a magic formula.
The lie no longer possesses the same monopoly on your silence.
And now they know what you mean when you answer.
Someone can remind you of the Gospel when shame starts screaming that failure is your identity.
Someone can help you distinguish conviction from condemnation.
And someone can look you in the eyes after hearing something you thought made you unlovable and remind you:
And He still went to the cross.
That does not make sin small.
Repentance is not pretending the wound never existed.
Grace does not rename darkness as light.
Grace meets us in darkness and leads us toward Christ.
This is why the Gospel Warrior theme matters so deeply:
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending the scandal never happened.
The thief beside Jesus really was guilty.
Human sin was so serious that redemption required the blood of the Son of God.
Yet sin does not get the final word over everyone who belongs to Christ.
Your worst chapter does not become good simply because you call it good.
He teaches people who spent years hiding how to walk in truth.
Maybe you have been waiting for the craving to disappear before telling someone.
Perhaps telling one safe person is one faithful step you have been postponing while you wait.
Not because that person can save you.
But the Christ who saves you also calls His people to bear one another's burdens, pray for one another, encourage one another, and walk together in the light.
You were never supposed to make another believer your savior.
But neither were you supposed to pretend you do not need the body of Christ.
So tonight, before you make another promise you may be too exhausted to keep alone, consider sending one message:
“Can we talk privately? There is something I've been fighting, and I don't want to hide anymore.”
Maybe your hands will shake when you send it.
Maybe you are afraid they will see you differently.
Choose wisely, then tell the truth.
Maybe shame tells you that real Christians do not struggle like this.
Real Christians are not people who never need repentance.
And the goal is not endless hiding followed by endless apologies with no desire to change.
Freedom increasingly expressed through a life surrendered to Him.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not owe the internet your private story.
But maybe you do need to stop telling yourself you can keep carrying it completely alone.
There may be another believer reading those same words tonight who thought they were the only one fighting.
Not as a badge of spirituality.
Because temptation has a way of making yesterday's convictions difficult to remember tomorrow night.
Come back when secrecy starts sounding reasonable again.
Jesus is not asking you to clean yourself well enough to deserve the cross.
The cross already announces that you could never save yourself.
Receive the forgiveness purchased by Christ.
Tell the truth to someone trustworthy.
Put practical boundaries around what keeps dragging you backward.
And when you stumble, do not turn your stumble into another hiding place.
Because perhaps the secret has been telling you, “If they ever know, everything is over.”
But the Gospel says something stronger:
When Jesus brings a sinner from darkness into grace, exposure does not have to become the end of the story—it can become the place where hiding finally loses its grip.
